identity.title: Unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash (or dermatomal allodynia preceding rash)

technique.how: Fully expose the painful region including back and flank. Look for grouped vesicles on an erythematous base confined to one or adjacent dermatomes, stopping sharply at the midline; in the pre-eruptive phase, test for dermatomal allodynia or hyperaesthesia with light touch. Re-examine in 1-3 days if pain is dermatomal but skin is clear.

interpretation.positive_finding: A unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption is diagnostic of herpes zoster on clinical grounds and explains dermatomal chest, abdominal or limb pain; disseminated lesions suggest immunocompromise.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of rash does not exclude zoster early on, since pain and allodynia precede the eruption by days (zoster sine herpete exists); it does not address cardiac or intra-abdominal causes.
interpretation.pitfalls: Prodromal zoster mimics ACS, pleurisy, cholecystitis or renal colic; early erythematous papules can be missed. Contact dermatitis or HSV can mimic; PCR of a lesion swab confirms atypical cases.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive rash establishes zoster: start antivirals within 72 h and stop cardiac/abdominal work-up unless features are discordant; if no rash, keep zoster on the list and re-examine.

sources.citation: Dworkin RH, Johnson RW, Breuer J, Gnann JW, Levin MJ, Backonja M, Betts RF, Gershon AA, et al. Recommendations for the management of herpes zoster. Clin Infect Dis. 2007;44 Suppl 1:S1-26.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute chest pain to zoster solely on the basis of pain when rash is absent and ACS/PE features are present.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Ophthalmic (V1) involvement, disseminated lesions, motor weakness, or immunocompromise require urgent specialist input and IV antivirals.

extraction_notes: No Rational Clinical Examination or diagnostic-accuracy study of the dermatomal rash as a bedside discriminator for chest/abdominal pain was found (searches: 'herpes zoster diagnosis accuracy clinical prospective PCR' returned only a laboratory PCR assay paper, PMID 26711555, not used). Zoster is diagnosed clinically per the IDSA-endorsed 2007 consensus recommendations (Dworkin et al.), cited as the guideline source. Estimates left empty; no numbers claimed.
